references.text: The immediate context where the religious leaders ask Jesus about his authority, and he responds with a counter-question about John's baptism ([ref:Luk 20:1-2|Luke 20:1-2]).
The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus asks the same question about whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men ([ref:Matt 21:25|Matthew 21:25]).
The parallel passage in Mark where Jesus asks if John's baptism was from heaven or from men ([ref:Mark 11:30|Mark 11:30]).

Luke describes how the people and tax collectors acknowledged that John's baptism was from God, while the Pharisees and teachers of the law rejected it – which sheds light on why Jesus asks this question ([ref:Luk 7:29-30|Luke 7:29-30]).
John testifies that he was sent by God to baptize with water, confirming that his baptism had a heavenly origin ([ref:Joh 1:33|John 1:33]).
The description of John's baptismal ministry and his call to repentance, showing that his service had divine origin ([ref:Matt 3:1-3|Matthew 3:1-3]).
The religious leaders' reaction to the question about John's baptism – they dared not answer because they feared the people, who regarded John as a prophet ([ref:Matt 21:26-27|Matthew 21:26-27]).

The leaders' internal deliberation and their evasive answer, showing that the question of the origin of John's baptism was decisive for the question of Jesus' authority ([ref:Luk 20:5-7|Luke 20:5-7]).

Luke's description that the word of God came to John, and that he preached a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins – showing that his baptism had divine authorization ([ref:Luk 3:2-3|Luke 3:2-3]).
John the Baptist himself says that no one can receive anything unless it is given from heaven, and confirms that he was sent ahead to prepare the way for Christ ([ref:Joh 3:27-28|John 3:27-28]).
